BASIS — every tracked file on origin/main @ 65e2843 (688 paths, 657 of them a language scc can name; the other 31 are binaries, dotfiles, and lockfiles — generated, and rightly left out) · scc 4.0.0 Code basis · counted 2026-09-11 · every number above imported from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-files.json · deliberately broader than the sheets' authored-source census, and deliberately main: this atlas's own branch would add a 29k-sloc self-portrait.

The source image — an isometric block city over a strategy-breeding harness — works because of three quiet decisions, and only one of them is the city: it maps roles in a mechanism rather than files; it spends its one visual scalar (height) on a true quantity; and it keeps a CONDITION field that says what is currently wrong. This set keeps those three decisions and lets everything else change with altitude.

The result is an argument about form: a loop where there is a genuine cycle (sheet 1), panels where packages are too small to be cities (sheet 2), the full city where the measurement thesis is actually true (sheet 3), a massed spine where the family shares one core but the limbs never touch (sheet 4), a chart where edges would be fiction (sheet 5), and mostly prose where only a definition survives (sheet 6). Fitness peaks in the middle altitudes and collapses at both ends.

Above the sixth altitude the set stops arguing about form and starts measuring. Sheets 7–10 are a survey quartet, each counting the same subject at a different boundary: what the repository holds (the monorepo by mass), what npm delivers (the sample app's node_modules, 297× the app it serves), what the browser downloads (the docs deploy on the wire, where prose and fonts outweigh every line of code), and who occupies the bytes after tree-shaking (the machine the router wraps is 22.5% of the bundle; the router itself, 3.9%). Sheet 11 cuts the same wire the other way, pricing five package quarters and sixteen doors one at a time. Sheet 12 leaves the wire and draws the monorepo as its own CI reads it, the pull-request task graph punched onto a register plate. Sheet 13 ages the city by commit date, and sheet 14 turns the instrument on itself: the census pipeline behind almost every number here, drawn as archive → probe stations → filed plates → drawings and introspected from the generator at build time. Interactive lanes (1i, 2B, 12i, 14i and the three.js city) walk the plates they sit beside; the appendix files plates whose subject is the atlas rather than the codebase.

the RENDER LOOP

ALTITUDE 1 — lit-ui-router 1.12.0 · the client circuit drawn as one isometric scene: every leg of the loop is a road on the grid, the document a browser window whose DOM rises in plates, and the five package entries a door strip along the footer · version read from census-files.json

GENERAL NOTES

Why redraw a 2D loop in 3D: the cycle itself is flat, but the third axis is free to carry the relations flat arrows kept fumbling. Containment: the child <ui-view> literally stands on its parent's roof — nesting is stacking, not a box-in-a-box. Propagation: uiSrefTarget events rise past the document's plates to the uiSrefActive perch, which is how link tracking works — no registry, just bubbling. Instrumentation: TransitionController is a skybridge that taps the hall without standing on the route.

The document breaks the metaphor on purpose. Every other station is a building; the document is drawn the way Firefox's old Tilt inspector drew it — a browser window whose DOM rises as stacked plates by depth, window → body → app shell → <ui-view> content → the <a> element on top. It is the one structure on this sheet that really is layered, so it alone earns the literal treatment.

Service discovery is still DOM events. A nested view finds its parent with a composed context CustomEvent; every uiSref announces its targetState upward. The document tree is the dependency graph — which is exactly why the drawing can stand everything in one window.

The five doors are one seam. The bare entry registers custom elements as a side effect; ./pure is the same API with registration torn off. sideEffects in the manifest names exactly the four register files.

the render loop (roads on the iso grid)
the click flying back to location
events rising / hook taps
plates = DOM depth (window → link)
elevated = overlay, not on the route
faint plate = scenery (your content)

STEP 0 / 12

BASIS — git archive origin/main @ 65e2843 — packages/lit-ui-router/src/{core.ts,transition-controller.ts,ui-router.ts,ui-sref-active.ts,ui-sref.ts,ui-view.ts} read line by line; every evidence line checked against its expected text by generator/census-loop.mjs · commit 2026-09-11 · 10 stations, 12 legs, 12 steps and 30 evidence lines read verbatim from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-loop.json; the ring is sheet 1's own order, computed at build time and drawn with cytoscape preset — no physics, so the picture is the same on every load.

GENERAL NOTES

Method — what is drawn, and from where. Everything on this page comes out of www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-loop.json, the checked-in plate generator/census-loop.mjs reads off a materialized archive of the ref — surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (commit 2026-09-11). It is a T1 tree probe: nothing runs, six files under packages/lit-ui-router/src/ are read line by line. The plate carries the 10 stations of sheet 1 (each anchored to the line where lit-ui-router implements it), the 12 legs between them (each with the call or event that carries it), and the walk — 12 steps, 30 evidence lines in all. Every evidence entry is filed as file:line plus the verbatim source at that line, and the probe throws if the line it was told to cite no longer reads what it expected: a refactor that moves a hook breaks this plate rather than letting it narrate stale code. The lane cross-checks the plate at build time and throws again if the walk names a leg that is not on it, a leg joins a station that is not on it, or the tallies disagree with the lists.

The walk, defined. One navigation: a click on <a uiSref> from /people to /people/32. The steps are ordered by the source, not by memory — the click handler's own guards and its $state.go, then core's sequence stated only through the hooks lit-ui-router registers in it: <ui-view>'s onBefore (uiCanExit) and onSuccess (uiOnParamsChanged), uiSrefActive's onStart tap and its trans.promise, TransitionController's default ['onSuccess']. No line of @uirouter/core is cited, so where the machine itself moves — matching, resolving, writing the url — the step says so and cites the wire lit-ui-router owns at that point. Step 2 is the click; step 1 is the circuit at rest, because before any click the stations have already found each other by composed DOM events, and that wiring is the only reason the click has anywhere to go.

Layout — sheet 1's ring, computed at build time. The stations stand in sheet 1's own order around a ring: location, core, the transition hall, the view with its child below it, Lit render, the document with the link on it. The two stations sheet 1 draws elevated — uiSrefActive and TransitionController — stand inside the ring here, because they are not on the route: sheet 1's key says "elevated = overlay", and inside is the flat drawing's word for the same thing. Positions are computed here and drawn with cytoscape preset: no physics, so a station is always in the same place when you come back to it. Loop legs run straight; the legs that would otherwise be read as passing through a building bow clear of it.

Sprites. Ten skins, one per station, authored to the house recipe — the girding frame drawn first and a semi-opaque wall washed over it, so the frame reads through and the themed node body tints the building. The document keeps sheet 1's one metaphor break: it is the only station that is not a building but a window with its DOM rising in plates, and the link is that topmost plate alone. Both palettes are baked at build time and swapped with the page's theme, the register's pattern exactly.

What this shows that sheet 1 cannot. Sheet 1 proves the loop is a circuit; here it has an order. The hall is tapped two times by the overlays and those taps fire at different bays — the perch hears onStart before any view has changed, the view hears onSuccess after every view has — which is why .active can flip before the page does. The two overlays never light a loop leg at all, in 12 steps. And the last step is honest about the one leg this package does not own: core writes the url; lit-ui-router's part of that wire is the listen() that carries the next back-button press in.

What is editorial. The ring and where the overlays stand; the sprite drawings and the colours; the narration sentences and this prose. The stations, the legs, the order of the steps, every line number, every excerpt and every count are the plate's.

the BRICK ASSEMBLY

ALTITUDE 2 — one baseplate, four bricks, 28 authored files · an exploded LEGO assembly with every coupling named to the API call that makes it, brick and stud faces drawn opaque so nothing reads through a mass in front of it · source counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Why bricks. The mechanism these packages share is a standardised coupling: each companion attaches to @uirouter/core through a published extension point, none of them attaches to another, and any one can be left in the box without disturbing the rest. That is a stud, and a stud is worth drawing. So this is an exploded isometric — the LEGO instruction manual's own idiom — with a numbered part per package, a drop line onto the exact stud it takes, and a parts callout. Nothing is drawn seated, because a seated assembly hides the undersides, and the undersides are the argument.

The plate is core, not this package. Sheet 4's finding decides it: every limb in the family declares @uirouter/core as a peer and touches nothing else. lit-ui-router is therefore brick 1, not the ground — and the drawing is honest about the one place the metaphor strains: class UIRouterLit extends UIRouter is moulded onto the plate, not snapped to it. What the drawing then shows is that the graft is thin anyway. Everything Lit-specific arrives through two published seams — this.plugin(servicesPlugin) and this.stateRegistry.decorator('views', litViewsBuilder) — plus urlService.listen()/sync() to start the thing. Three calls, and one internal seam — viewService._pluginapi._viewConfigFactory('lit', …) — that core does not publish. That is the whole renderer coupling.

One stud is a seat, not a socket. router.plugin() is the back rail: a single method that anything may queue on, which is why the spare-parts box is drawn at all — @uirouter/visualizer, sticky-states, dsr and rx all register through it and none of them knows this repo exists. One seat on that rail is ringed red, because it behaves differently: a router holds exactly one location plugin, so ui-router-navigation-location-plugin is a swap for core's pushStateLocation, never an addition. That package peers @uirouter/core and nothing else — it has never heard of Lit, and would work identically under the React or Angular adapters.

Brick 3 is the only brick-to-brick coupling in the set, and it is a small one. lit-ui-router-mobx seats on brick 1 through UIRouterLitElement.seekRouter(host) — a bubbling ui-router-context event, published precisely as the dependency-injection primitive for external reactivity systems — and then reaches the plate directly: one transitionService.onSuccess({}, update) hook, memoised one-per-router by RouterStore.for(), whose update() reads globals.current, globals.params and the last successful transition into MobX observables. It observes; it never writes router state. 176 lines, one stud on the brick above and two on the plate below.

The fourth brick has no stud here at all, and that is the design. ui-router-server declares @uirouter/core as an optional peer (peerDependenciesMeta); its default 'matcher' tier is dependency-free pattern matching and never loads core, and its 'simulate' tier reaches a plate of its own behind a lazy import() — new UIRouter() with servicesPlugin and memoryLocationPlugin, built fresh per resolution because core mutates registrations. Drawing it over a dashed second plate is the only truthful placement: it is the same mould, a different assembly, and the tie back to the client plate is crossed out.

Massing, quantized. Continuous mass would have made these bricks unbuildable shapes, so the census is rounded to LEGO: plan is one stud per 150 sloc rounded up to the next standard shape (1×1, 1×2, 2×2, 2×3, 2×4), height is one course per three authored files. The result is legible and it is a finding — the two bricks that carry a renderer and a server are 2×4s; the two that plug the router into something are a 1×1 and a 1×2 tile, 105 and 176 lines. A companion that needed to be a 2×4 would be lit-ui-router's problem to absorb, not a package. The baseplate is deliberately not massed: 80 files and 5,272 lines of core is ground, and ground has no height.

The fifth published package is not a brick. eslint-plugin-lit-ui-router 1.0.1 (10 files, 771 sloc) ships from this repo alongside the four drawn here, but it takes no stud on any router plate: it couples to ESLint and oxlint, not to @uirouter/core, so it is scheduled as row 5 and left off the drawing. Every number on this sheet is read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-bricks.json — counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11).

ALTITUDE 2 — ALTERNATE PLATE: the same four companions as sheet 2, laid out for reading — core central as a socket wall, companions at its right, the server below the no-DOM line — with every coupling drawn disengaged and lettered to its API call · rows read census-bricks.json @ 65e2843

GENERAL NOTES

This plate is the legibility companion to sheet 2. The exploded assembly (sheet 2, THE BRICK ASSEMBLY) shows the whole stack and where every brick falls; this plate isolates the couplings and draws each one at reading size. The arrangement answers to reading rather than to assembly — core central, companions at its right, the server in a request lane below the no-DOM line — and the packages are shallow solids, so the recovered space goes entirely to the joints.

Every joint is drawn disengaged. A seated plug hides both mating faces, so nothing here is seated: each stud on the wall stops 18px short of its plug’s mouth, the dashed centreline is the engagement, and the call that makes the coupling — stateRegistry.decorator('views', litViewsBuilder), urlService.listen()/.sync(), router.plugin(servicesPlugin), transitionService.onSuccess({}, update), globals.current/.params — is lettered on the connection itself, not in a schedule at the edge of the sheet.

One connection point is a seat, not a stud, and it is drawn as a keyed recess. A router holds exactly one location plugin, so ui-router-navigation-location-plugin does not add to the wall — it swaps: its keyed red plug approaches the LOCATION SEAT while a dashed ghost plug, core’s own pushStateLocation, leaves it. The rail above behaves the opposite way: router.plugin() is one method with any number of seats, which is where visualizer, sticky-states, dsr and rx would queue (sheet 4).

The one brick-to-brick coupling gets its own axis. lit-ui-router-mobx is the only companion that touches another companion: its upward socket waits under a stud on lit-ui-router’s underside — seekRouter(host), the bubbling ui-router-context event — and everything else it does is read-only against the wall: one memoised onSuccess hook on stud C, observations of globals on stud E, never a write.

The missing coupling is drawn only to be crossed out. ui-router-server takes no stud: @uirouter/core is an optional peer (peerDependenciesMeta), its default 'matcher' tier is dependency-free, and its 'simulate' tier lazily imports a wall of its own. Blocks are sized roughly by mass — front-face area ≈ 35 px² per sloc, from census-bricks.json counted at origin/main @ 65e2843, which puts lit-ui-router at 1,399 sloc — with the two smallest companions (1×1 and 1×2) clamped up to a legible minimum, because at true scale they would be postage stamps, and their smallness is already sheet 2’s finding.

the INSTRUMENT YARD

ALTITUDE 3 — 5 publishable packages · 23 tools · 76 turbo task names · one packer, many readers · every mass counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-yard.json on scc Code lines — 208 authored files and 14,458 sloc across 17 massed structures, with the task-manager inset reading the same two plates sheet 3A draws

GENERAL NOTES

Method — one basis, shared with sheet 4. Every massed structure was counted from this repo's authored source, counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) and read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-yard.json: .ts/.tsx/.js/.mjs under each member's source directory, excluding *.d.ts, *.test-d.ts, *.spec.* and *.test.*, specs/, __tests__/ and fixtures. sloc is scc's Code count — string-aware, so the interior of a template literal counts as code rather than as one line. @tools/release hosts several instruments at once, so it is attributed by module prefix — check-published-diff* to structure 11, check-exports* to 10, the pack modules to 3, the release steps to 5 — with every file landing in exactly one structure and none counted twice. 19 structures, 17 of them massed: 208 authored files, 14,458 lines. One member is massed nowhere: @tools/wintercg-globals is a single globals.d.ts, and declaration files are outside this basis. The tarball, the registry and the boundary are diagrammatic.

Mass is volume; volume does not predict authority. Footprint side is 1.6 · √sloc, so plan area tracks lines; height is 1.5 px per authored file, so a block's volume is its sloc × files. The two heaviest masses on the sheet are material: the sample apps (56 files, 3,171 lines) and packages/*/src (38 files, 3,592 lines). The 5 structures that can stop a pull request total 20 files between them, and one of them — dts-backtest — is a single 291-line run.ts. Encoding severity as height would imply the opposite; the census says a gate's authority has nothing to do with how much code it is.

Severity in colour. Red hatch across cap and flank marks a check that stops the PR line: the vitest harness (7), compat-guards (8), dts-backtest (9), check:exports (10) and Cypress e2e (17). One block is solid red — published-diff (11) — because it is the only structure that halts publishing itself, and it closes the loop by pulling the live npm tarball back for comparison, which makes the registry part of the circuit rather than a destination. Accent hatch marks the gates that fire later rather than on a PR: peer-floor tier-2 (12) gates version bumps, the workers-builds watch (19) gates the docs deploy. Faint, unhatched blocks never gate at all — peer-floor tier-1 reports check runs, the lint & probe fleet is advisory, @tools/shared and the typedoc plugin are libraries. The tiers survive both themes because they differ in hatch as well as hue: solid red, red hatch, accent hatch, no hatch.

One packer, many readers (#449). The dashed trunk leaving the green crate is literal: check:exports (publint + attw), dts-backtest and published-diff all read the same cached packPublishTarball output. No check re-packs, so a drift verdict is always about the artifact that would actually ship. Known failure mode, drawn nowhere but real: a poisoned remote cache entry can replay a stale verdict — --force is the remediation.

Two task managers, one re-entrant loop. The inset at top left is drawn flat, not isometric, because a task manager is not a place — and because the relationship is not the clean layering it sounds like. GitHub Actions enters mise at 37 call sites across 8 workflows (28 distinct tasks); mise itself is almost graphless — 51 tasks with exactly 2 of them declaring depends (5 edges), lint_workflows → its four linters and setup → turbo_link_worktree — because it delegates fan-out rather than modelling it. Seven mise tasks shell turbo, whose ci graph alone expands to 660 task nodes. Then the loop closes back on itself: seven root package.json scripts shell mise run again, so turbo's //#lint:markdown node literally runs mise run lint_markdown. That return is the whole point — mise/aqua owns the versions of the non-node tools (rumdl, taplo, shellcheck, actionlint, zizmor), and turbo climbs back out to it to get a cache key over tools node never installs. Neither gantry is above the other.

the HANDOFF WORKS

ALTITUDE 3 · ALTERNATE PLATE — the sheet-3 task-manager inset at full size: 8 of 12 workflows · 51 mise tasks in 4 homes · turbo ci 660 nodes, 195 real · 4 seam types · 3 service doors · every frame sized to the widest DIN line it holds, so the spine is computed rather than hand-set · every count imported from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-handoff.json + census-plate.json · counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Method — one census, cited throughout. Every count on this plate is imported: www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-handoff.json for the workflows, the mise tasks and the turbo definitions, census-plate.json for the graph. Both are written by probes that read a materialized archive of the ref — the 12 workflow files, the 19 turbo.json files, .config/mise/** and both member mise.toml files — with the graph figures from a bare turbo run ci --dry=json on an installed archive. No mise or turbo runs on this machine to draw it, and nothing numeric here is hand-pasted: the task-name lists, the cited file:lines and this prose are the editorial part. Basis: counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11); graph surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) · turbo 2.10.12.

The star fitting: turbo caches mise. Six root //# scripts in the ci graph have mise run … as their literal command, and their turbo inputs explicitly hash .config/mise/tasks/* and .config/mise/mise.lock (turbo.json:264-268, 281-287, 292-298); a seventh port, @tools/release#check:release-closure, re-enters from a member script and hashes config.toml the same way (tools/release/turbo.json:39-50). That is the whole trade drawn as one gasket on the return duct: mise owns the tool versions (taplo, rumdl, shellcheck, actionlint, zizmor — none installable by node), turbo owns the cache, and the gasket hashes one machine against the other, so a taplo pin bump invalidates exactly the taplo lane and nothing else.

A DAG in a loop costume. The circuit workflow → mise → turbo → mise looks re-entrant, but the 51 tasks partition cleanly: the seven that shell turbo (★ — ci, ci_main, build, codecov_bundle, dts_backtest_matrix, check_pack, published_diff) are reachable only from workflows and humans, while the eight turbo re-enters (↩ — the lint and format tasks, and check_release_closure) only exec pinned binaries, file tasks or a manifest reader. No edge leads from the second set back to the first. The deepest chain is six hops and runs on every PR, four tool lanes in parallel: workflow YAML → mise run ci → turbo run ci → //#lint:toml → mise run lint_toml → the taplo file task → the pinned binary.

Three service doors, all deliberate. deflake-e2e.yml:73 runs bare turbo run build --filter=… — over the umbrella, though mise still supplies the PATH; deflake-e2e.yml:87 runs the flake attempts through pnpm outside turbo, because a cached test task would replay attempt 1’s logs; and the production docs deploy never sees mise at all — Cloudflare Workers Builds clears corepack’s shims and installs pnpm@12.2.1 globally through npm before npx turbo docs#build (tools/workers-builds/cloudflare-build.sh:26-38), because the hosted image’s corepack shim cannot materialize pnpm 12. The doors are drawn red and hatched because each one gives up something the machines provide — and each was opened on purpose.

Two curiosities the census surfaced. One task in the whole machine is dead: //tools/build_and_test:playwright_deps (mise.toml:72-76) has no caller anywhere, superseded by playwright_deps_engines. And one umbrella exists twice: mise lint_workflows (a 4-leg depends, config.toml:139-143) and turbo //#lint:workflows (a virtual with node, turbo.json:251-261) are the same shape maintained by hand in both schedulers — the one place the two machines duplicate rather than delegate. The phantom shroud around turbo’s core — 465 of 660 nodes that exist only to carry hashes — is drawn as wall thickness here; sheet 12 punches it hole by hole.

ALTITUDE 3 · ALTERNATE PLATE B — the PR ci graph as a city: 195 real tasks in 26 massed structures · footprint = watched files (9,479 task-file hashes) · height = command sloc (2,212) · 465 phantom plots · every number imported from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-mass3b.json, surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Method — the graph, imported. Every mass and footprint on this plate is read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-mass3b.json, the checked-in snapshot census-mass3b.mjs writes from a bare turbo run ci --dry=json on an installed archive of the ref — surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11), turbo 2.10.12: 660 nodes, 195 real, 1,544 edges, 73 real→real. Nothing below is hand-pasted; a structure whose tasks have left the plate throws at build time rather than drawing a stale number, and the schedule totals are the plate's own sums. Footprint is the per-task inputs map — the files whose hashes decide that task's cache key — at 1.2·√files per side. Height is command mass: the package.json script line plus the repo script or bin file it executes, sloc-counted by census-mass3b.mjs on scc 4.0.0's Code basis (guards, emitters and mise task files each cited in the schedule; external binaries like tsc and oxlint contribute only their one line, because that is all this repo wrote). Wall-clock and cache-hit rates are excluded as geometry by design: they are properties of runs, not of the graph.

The city is flat, and that is the finding. 155 of 195 real tasks have command mass 1 — one script line handing the work to a pinned binary. The whole city executes 2,212 sloc of repo-written command while watching 9,479 task-file hashes. The skyline is inverted from intuition: @tools/dts-backtest#test is a 291-line run.ts on a 32-file lot — sheet 3 calls it "one 291-line run.ts holds the TS 5.0 floor", and the graph survey agrees to the line — while the largest footprint, the examples plain, watches 303 files (format:check 61 + lint 61 alone) under 19 lines of command. The tallest command is the root yard's //#lint:elements, the one root lane that runs a repo-written bin rather than an external one — 186 sloc over warn-lanes.core.ts's 214 — a 401-sloc spire on a root-surface footprint. The eslint-plugin quarter is flat throughout: eslint-plugin-lit-ui-router brings 9 tasks and 85 sloc, and all but its two oxc-emit build lanes are one line apiece.

The root yard repays the walk. All 13 //# plots are drawn individually, and six of them — lint:root, typecheck:root, lint:elements, format:check:root, lint:templates and lint:package-json — are equal slabs watching one identical root surface of 688 files. Six tasks, one surface, one number: it is the plate's cleanest finding. The guards that patrol that surface are not root tasks: @tools/repo-checks is a package, drawn whole as the guard house (1) standing off the yard's west edge, and four of its 8 tasks — check:graph-edges, check:task-inputs, check:patches and check:knip — are named in the lint task's with list, so a lint run drags them along wherever it starts. Three of the four are the city's tall one-file guards, 124, 97 and 70 lines of TypeScript apiece; the fourth is one knip line hashing 516 files, the widest lot in the block. The taplo pad (12) is where plate 3A's six-hop chain touches ground: hops ①–② arrive from mise run ci, hop ③ is this block, and ④–⑥ leave immediately to run back inside mise through the cache gasket. And one lot in the yard is vacant on purpose — //#lint:workflows, the virtual with twin, has no command even here.

One tier, uniformly red. Sheet 3's severity vocabulary survives, but at this altitude it degenerates truthfully: every real node in the ci graph stops the PR when it fails, so every massed block wears the same red hatch, and the drawing spends its information elsewhere. The 5 ci:main-only tasks (test:engines ×3, check:pack, test:matrix) sit outside this survey on an unmassed accent annex — 697/200 nodes when they are included; the 465 phantom plots — 70.5% of the graph, transit and ^build hash carriers — are the vacant field behind the city, inventoried hole-by-hole on sheet 12.

Roads and reach. Five arteries are drawn, one per district pair, and the plate labels them with degree rather than with an edge tally it cannot cite: @www/lit-ui-router.dev#build waits on 14 nodes (every quarter ships docs:api there, plus worker types and app fixtures — it is the city's sink), @tools/typedoc-plugin-lit-ui-router#build:types unblocks 24, @tools/release#check:exports 35 (pack:all and check:exports read every quarter), and the widest fan-out in the graph is lit-ui-router#build:types at 32. Of the graph's 1,544 edges only 73 join two real tasks; the rest hang off phantom transit nodes, which is why the roads are drawn as districts and not as a wire count.

One gate is red: @uirouter/react pins core at exactly 6.1.2 and ships it as a dependency, not a peer — the only limb that can install a second copy of the state machine into a consumer's tree, and the only one that cannot be moved forward without a react release.

Mass does not track liveness. The largest limb on the sheet is the dormant @uirouter/visualizer (34 files, 2,018 lines, last published 2020-09-19) — it carries a preact/d3 rendering stack, so it out-masses every living adapter. The newest limb, lit-ui-router, is 14 files and 1,399 lines at 1.12.0, and it is the only limb growing limbs of its own: the companion bay adds another 1,422 lines behind a single shared gate, with lit-ui-router-mobx the one package on this sheet that peers a limb as well as the spine.

Publish dates sort the family into three states. @uirouter/angular stands at 22.0.0 (2026-08-18), a major of its own, so it is drawn active; angularjs and react carry only the 2025-12-31 patch wave that followed core inside a day, so they are drawn wave. Below the rail nothing is current — the newest instrument publish is rx at 2021-11-30, the rest 2019–2020 — and the dashes say so. @uirouter/vue holds a seat with no registry row at all: an absence, not a package.

the DESIGN SPACE

ALTITUDE 5 — ten routers placed by where matching happens and who owns navigation, shape marking the source of truth · positions are editorial, argued in the notes

GENERAL NOTES

This altitude forbids the city outright. A diagram's edges assert mechanism, and there is none between TanStack and SvelteKit. The honest form is a positioned chart whose axes are real, contested design decisions — with the positions owned as editorial judgment, not measurement.

Reading the columns: the field has been sliding left for a decade — filesystem routes and typegen move matching toward build time; server components move it toward the server. The client-runtime column is where the platform itself now competes, via the Navigation API.

The square is the argument. Every circle on this chart treats the URL as the source of truth and derives the view from it. The ui-router lineage inverts that: a named, hierarchical state tree is primary, and the URL is a projection — one of several possible addresses for a state. That inversion is why sheet 1's loop runs through a state registry rather than a path matcher, and why the same tree can answer HTTP requests in sheet 2's server lane. It is also why the square sits alone: the niche is real, small, and — for state-heavy embedded UIs where the address bar is not the whole story — defensible.

the ROUTING STRATA

ALTITUDE 6 — routing in general · the altitude where prose outranks pictures

GENERAL NOTES

The definition that survives every stratum: a router is an address space, a matching function, and transition semantics. BGP matches prefixes and forwards with no memory; an HTTP framework matches path patterns into a stateless response; an edge ruleset rewrites and proxies; a SPA router matches a URL into a view tree through a cancellable lifecycle; a state router matches into a named hierarchy through guarded, resolving transitions.

What changes with ascent is the transition. At the bedrock a transition is a forwarding decision that forgets itself immediately. Each stratum upward, transitions acquire more: statefulness, interceptability, cancellation, resolved data, meaning. By the surface a transition is a first-class object with a lifecycle — which is precisely the layer sheet 1 drew.

Why this sheet is mostly writing: no mechanism spans these strata — an IP hop and a ui-view activation share a definition, not a wire. Drawing more than a core sample here would be decoration, and the reference's own rule applies: the drawing earns exactly as much ink as the mechanism deserves.

ALTITUDE 3½ — the same city as sheet 3, surveyed by mass · 35 members in 4 districts, footprint ∝ √sloc, height ∝ authored files, spec mass drawn as an annex, gate severity in colour · counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Method — one basis, two series. Every count on this sheet is read at build time from the checked-in plate www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-city.json, counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11): .ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.mjs under each member's source directory, excluding *.d.ts, *.test-d.ts, fixtures, dist/ and node_modules/; sloc is scc's Code count — string-aware, so the interior of a template literal counts as code rather than as one line. Sheet 3 throws test code away; this sheet does not — anything matching *.{spec,test,cy}.* or living under specs/ test/ tests/ __tests__/ cypress/ is counted into a second series and drawn as that member's annex. 35 members: 241 authored files and 18,823 sloc of source, plus 106 files and 15,710 sloc of spec. The packages district's five buildings reconcile exactly with sheet 3's source slab — 38 files, 3,592 lines — because both are queries over one census rather than two hand counts.

Every shipped building carries an annex bigger than itself. lit-ui-router: 1,399 authored lines against 4,250 of spec (3.0×). ui-router-server: 1,141 vs 2,174 (1.9×). lit-ui-router-mobx: 176 vs 453 (2.6×). eslint-plugin-lit-ui-router: 771 vs 1248 (1.6×). navigation-location-plugin is one 105-line file with 7 spec files over it (3.9×). The test budget lives exactly where the repo says it should — in packages/*, and nowhere else at that ratio.

Every road is citable. Solid roads are build edges: packages/* into the sample apps, the apps into docs, @tools/oxc-emit into all five packages — each a workspace: dependency, each backed by turbo's build/docs tasks depending on ^build. Dashed soft roads are the test lane: @tools/dts-backtest depends on the four runtime packages and backtests their emitted d.ts against the TS 5.0 floor; @tools/lit-test-env and @tools/happy-dom run up into lit-ui-router's annex because they are its devDependencies and the harness its suites load; sample-app-lit-e2e depends on docs, and turbo's e2e depends on ^build and runs with docs#wrangler:dev, so Cypress drives the built shopfront under its worker rather than a vite dev server. The accent road is the one that leaves a member twice — once from the source block and once from the spec annex — because the package's typecheck reads both: tsconfig.json includes src/**, specs and all (only the narrower typecheck:src excludes them), while the ^build:types dependency is what carries the result into the next district. One faint road stands for eight: that many instruments import @tools/shared, whose src/globs.ts (#655) holds the custom-element glob three lanes share. Only the road to the largest is drawn, because drawing all eight would turn the yard into hatching.

Severity in colour, mass in geometry — and they disagree. The tiers are sheet 3's, applied to whole members: @tools/release is solid red because it hosts published-diff, the only structure that halts a publish; red hatch marks the seven members that can stop a pull request — Cypress e2e, dts-backtest, compat-guards, lit-test-env, happy-dom, lint-elements, whose ratchet exits non-zero on a new warning, and repo-checks, whose graph-edge, task-input, knip and patch guards ride the lint lane; accent hatch marks @tools/workers-builds, which gates the docs deploy and nothing earlier. Here the two encodings happen to agree once, on release, and disagree everywhere else: the harness that can stop every pull request in the repo is 8 authored lines of @tools/happy-dom, sitting on the drawing's minimum footprint.

What the districts say. The product is 5 modest buildings — 3,592 lines — against 7,657 in the instrument yard and 3,234 in the proving ground. The broadest source block on the sheet is examples — 3,655 lines of stackblitz copies — with sample-app-shared, which ships to nobody and gates nothing, just behind at 2,261; the only footprint that outbuilds both is lit-ui-router's spec annex. @tools/wintercg-globals is drawn on the floor with no mass at all: it is ambient types, and a census that hides its empty members is not a census.

Every count above and on the drawing is read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-city.json, the snapshot census-city.mjs writes out of the master per-file census; this module holds placement, tiers and prose only. The plate is measured at a named ref rather than at whatever a working tree happens to hold — counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) — so every number here is citable to a committed file, and a member the sheet draws but the plate does not carry is a build error rather than a stale constant.

the SHADOW SURVEY

ALTITUDE 3½ — ALTERNATE PLATE TO SHEET 7: the measured city under its own test light · same city as sheet 7, 35 members · reach = the source each suite loads, brightness = line coverage of what it loads · metered at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Method — one meter per member, nothing installed by hand, nothing left behind. Footprints, annexes and districts are sheet 7's own plate (census-city.json); the light is census-shadow.json, metered at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11), so meter and census read one tree at one ref. 20 of the 35 members carry a meter. The probe never edits a repo file: members that declare test:coverage are metered by the tree's own unmodified turbo run test:coverage; node:test members by their own test script re-run with --experimental-test-coverage and the lcov reporter; the vitest members by their own script with --coverage.enabled --coverage.provider=v8. Each meter reports lines on its own basis (v8 remaps to executable lines; node counts raw lines), so brightness percentages are per-meter and are never summed across meters in the drawing — only the schedule's grand total does, and says so. LIT means a source file the suite actually executed; extent is those files' sloc over the member's src sloc, both from the same ref. One honest wobble found by re-running the probe four times over: node --test's branch denominator for №31 came back 213 on two runs and 215 on two more, with 191 hit either way — a 0.9-point swing on one member's branch figure and nothing else in the plate moved. Branch discovery under V8 is not perfectly repeatable, and this plate says so rather than pretending the last run is the only one.

The product glows wall to wall — the budget lands where the house says. The published packages meter 99.3% of 3,463 lines over 97.5% of their metered source. What little stays dark is entry barrels and interface.ts — type declarations, which no runtime meter can light. This is the priority made visible: library coverage outranks docs coverage, and the annexes sheet 7 drew at 1.5–3.9× their buildings turn out to buy near-total light.

The yard's habit: bright cores, dark wrappers. The instruments repeat one pattern — @tools/release, build_and_test, workers-builds, lcov-rebase: the .core.ts logic is lit and the command-line file in front of it is not. 2,508 sloc across 47 files of process-edge code is never loaded by any suite, while the logic behind it meters 97.9%. compat-guards is the pattern at its extreme: only ranges.ts is unit-lit; its guard lanes run for real in CI, where no meter follows. @tools/happy-dom is the survey's one genuine surprise: it owns a lit lamp and still stands dark, because its spec is a conformance canary pointed at happy-dom upstream — its own append.ts is lit only from lit-ui-router's lamp, as borrowed light.

What the meter cannot say, the plate refuses to fake. The two demo apps and the Cypress host are hatched in accent, not banded: e2e light is real — the rig drives the built docs site — but no lcov leaves it, so it is drawn as light of unknowable brightness and labelled unmetered. That judgement is the only one in the probe, and it is verified rather than assumed: the run throws if the rig has stopped being a Cypress suite. sample-app-shared runs its unit tests green, yet browser-mode vitest cannot fetch a coverage provider the repo never installed; its light is an outline, and the probe proves it by running the suite a second time without the meter. The members that are dark are dark because nothing tests them, and two of them (dts-backtest, lit-test-env) spend their working lives inside other members' suites.

ALTITUDE 3½ — SYNTHESIS PLATE TO SHEET 7: the census city as a working plant · weathering (13) × test light (7A) × gates (7) × live build, one sprite per member · steam window 2026-06-13..2026-09-11 · counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

The sprite decorates; the census governs. Every block is sheet 7's, unchanged: footprint 1.6·√sloc, height 3 px per authored file, spec annexes beside their buildings, gate severity in the same colours with the same uniform hatch including the cap. The Working Plant sprite (concept 3 of the sprite studies) adds four state channels as overlays. The design guard from the study is enforced: rust is a dotted speckle at partial opacity on the flanks only — never the cap, never a 45° line hatch — so a red-gated pristine plant (uniform hatch, cap included) and a rusting never-gating plant cannot be confused, in either theme.

Every channel is measured, and every threshold comes from a distribution. RUST is sheet 13's weathering census: median days since last touch per member, five steps cut where the idle histogram cuts — 0 ≤14d · R1 ≤30 · R2 ≤37 · R3 ≤58 · R4 >180. The top step spans a band nothing occupies (61–180 days), so R4 means genuinely sealed, and only the typedoc plugin wears it. STEAM is distinct commits touching the member in a trailing 90-day window, read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-steam.json — window 2026-06-13..2026-09-11, counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) — banded 0 puffs ≤2 · 1: 3–8 · 2: 9–15 · 3: ≥16. Those edges are editorial: 3, 9 and 16 are all occupied on this window, so they sit in traffic rather than in empty air. Six plants steam at three puffs: lit-ui-router (36), sample-app-shared (29), docs (6), @tools/release (26), sample-app-lit-e2e (23) and examples (19). LAMPS compress plate 7A's meter to one number — lit share = extent × line coverage — read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-shadow.json, metered at origin/main @ 65e2843: three lamps at ≥90, two at ≥50, one above zero, and the accent lamp is 7A's honest category for light no meter reads. PIPES are the turbo run build graph from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-plate.json: 24 real tasks in 124 nodes, last run green on 2026-08-17 (all cache hits — a replay of green, stated as such), so every pipe on the sheet connects and the key says so rather than inventing a broken one.

The channels disagree, which is the point. A single wreck-to-splendor axis would have to average these stories away. lit-ui-router is the oldest masonry in the city and its hottest steam and fully lamped — old and running. The typedoc plugin is the only R4 rust on the sheet, cracked flanks and all, yet still emits a puff, because index.ts takes commits while symbols/ sleeps its 234 days. examples steams at 3 puffs with zero lamps and only R1 rust — worked on, untested, barely aging — while docs pairs the city's second-hottest steam with its dimmest metered light (10.8% lit). And @tools/happy-dom keeps plate 7A's strangest fact: a plant with its own spec annex and no lamp lit, because the spec is a canary pointed upstream.

Three channels by import, one by hand. Placements, districts and gate tiers are imported from sheet 7's own placement table, and the masses from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-city.json, so the two sheets cannot drift building for building. Steam, lamps and pipes are each looked up by member directory in their own filed plate, and a member this sheet draws that a plate does not carry is a build error rather than a stale number. Rust is the exception: an editorial step per member, keyed by badge off sheet 13's weathering census and labelled as such wherever it is printed. The steam total — 299 member-touches from 447 window commits — double-counts commits touching several members, as any per-member count must, so the window commit count is printed beside it.

ALTITUDE 1½ — what npm actually installs for one consumer · sample-app-lit-vanilla · 32 delivered packages, 177,392 lines of code and 39,963 d.ts lines on disk, footprint from files and height from lines — measured at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11), closure of apps/sample-app-lit-vanilla

GENERAL NOTES

Method: the production closure of apps/sample-app-lit-vanilla (dependencies plus installed peers — pnpm auto-installs peers, so they are genuinely on disk), resolved through the pnpm store and measured as delivered: lines of .js/.ts/.css/.html per package directory, source maps and prose excluded, .d.ts drawn separately as the hatched annex. Workspace-linked members are measured by their built dist/ — the shape a registry install would deliver. Plenty of prior art measures this differently — bundlephobia and packagephobia weigh tarballs and install bytes, npmgraph draws the dependency graph — but this sheet measures what actually lands on disk, in files and lines, and stages it as a city with the consumer's own building standing in it for scale. Every count on the drawing and in these notes is read at build time from the plate www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-nm.json — measured at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11), closure of apps/sample-app-lit-vanilla — written after installing and building the ref itself, never the working tree. A package the drawing places that the plate does not carry, or a package the plate carries that no district draws, is a build error rather than a stale constant.

The consumer is a doormat in its own city. The app brings 592 lines of its own and receives 177,392 delivered lines of code plus 39,963 of type declarations — 300× its own mass. The router this repo exists to ship, lit-ui-router, delivers 1,535 lines over 28 files: one of the smaller buildings on the skyline it anchors, and 116× smaller than the city it stands in.

Four imports, 22,193 lines. lodash-es is delivered whole — 22,193 lines across 644 files — so the app can call isEqual, cloneDeep, get and set. The bundler tree-shakes almost all of it away, and sheet 9 charts what survives to the wire; the delivered city is the other measure, the one that installs, audits and updates. It is the fourth-tallest building here, behind dompurify, hono and @uirouter/core.

One lit, and a server in a client demo. Scoped pnpm overrides (@api-viewer/docs>lit, @api-viewer/common>lit, lit-dialog>lit → ^3.3.3) hold the demo chrome to one lit major, so lit, lit-html, lit-element and @lit/reactive-element each stand once in this city. The oddest building is hono at 30,768 lines: ui-router-server names it a peer, so peer auto-install delivers a server framework into a client demo.

Note the vertical scale: 1 px ≈ 250 lines against sheet 7's ≈ 34. Drawn at the workspace's own scale, lodash-es alone would stand 653 px tall — the compression is the finding.

ALTITUDE 2¾ — what the browser downloads · lit-ui-router.dev, one deploy · 579 files in 11 districts, 3.5 MB on the wire, footprint from file count and height from gzipped bytes — measured at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) · www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/generator/census-shipped.mjs

GENERAL NOTES

Method: every number on this sheet is read at build time from the checked-in plate www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-shipped.json — measured at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) · www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/generator/census-shipped.mjs. The probe builds www/lit-ui-router.dev/dist inside a materialized, installed archive of the ref, never the working tree, and measures it file by file: height is gzip level 9 of each file, the honest wire measure, since the CDN serves compressed. Footprint is file count, as on sheets 7 and 8. A reachability walk — every HTML shell and hashed chunk, following static asset references — sorts the assets into districts, and a shared chunk counts where it is first claimed (vanilla → mobx → hash), because the CDN ships it once. This sheet extends the survey a step further: sheet 7 measures the source, sheet 8 what npm delivers, this sheet what one deploy actually ships — 579 files, 15.6 MB on disk, 3.5 MB on the wire. Sheet 10 goes one level in again and opens the bundle itself.

The tallest building is the prose. The skyline is the site's 135 prerendered HTML pages at 845 KB, with Inter's 16 woff2 faces 2,942 bytes ahead at 848 KB — a race close enough that a few new guides decide it. Code does not crack the top two: on the wire, this documentation site is mostly prose and typography, and the first script district — the examples, led by one galaxy — stands third at 1034 KB. A vacant lot at the plan's edge marks where the demo corpora stood; they are no longer shipped.

The product is a guest in its own city. The three routed sample apps — the thing the site exists to demonstrate — total 200 KB gzipped, 5.6% of the deploy. First claim seats visualizer.esm and the custom-elements manifest in app: vanilla, which is why that district reads 18 files and 120 KB while the hash app's whole district is 4 files and 14.7 KB. Two rules shape those numbers rather than the CDN: a scoped override holds the @api-viewer/lit-dialog stack to one lit major, so identical lit chunks hash identically across apps and part of mobx's download is chunks vanilla already ships; and the api-viewer docs panel, which renders only behind a feature flag, arrives in a lazy api-docs chunk rather than the eager main one. Same bytes on the CDN, fewer on the critical path.

There is no ghost district. The reachability walk follows the backtick-quoted asset URLs the app chunks build by hand, so the api-viewer custom-elements manifest is reachable after all, and the orphan list on this plate is empty — no hatched block stands here. Read that as a statement about the instrument as much as the deploy: an orphan count is only as good as the walk that produces it, and earlier walks over an accumulated local dist/ reported orphans that were stale build output, not shipped weight. This census builds clean, into a materialized archive of the ref, and counts what a browser can reach.

One example outweighs the router. The examples district — 22 files, 1034 KB — is led by the hellogalaxy demo's model-viewer chunk at 275 KB on its own, heavier than all three sample apps combined, delivered so one tutorial page can spin a galaxy.

ALTITUDE 2⅞ — inside the wire: what the bundler kept · one production bundle: 14 package groups in 17 chunks, 120,477 gz, footprint from source kept and height from wire share — apps/sample-app-lit-vanilla · counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Method: a generateBundle census on a real production vite build of apps/sample-app-lit-vanilla, run inside a materialized, installed archive of the measured ref rather than the working tree — apps/sample-app-lit-vanilla · counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11). Every rendered module is attributed to its package by an explicit grouping table whose misses land in a loud other row (this print: none), and every footprint, height, schedule row and door price is read from the checked-in plates at build time — a group the drawing places that the plate does not carry is a build error, not a stale constant. Footprint is post-tree-shake source kept; height is generateBundle: module renderedLength scaled by its chunk gz/rendered ratio — the honest wire share. Beside it, the repo's own codecov bundle-analysis probe (tools/bundle-probe, the <pkg>-<label>-esm series CI uploads) prices each exported entry at the same ref, read here from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-doors.json. This closes the survey as a quartet: the source (7), what npm delivers (8), what the wire carries (9) — and here, who occupies those bytes. Sheet 11 is this sheet's split view: the same probe cut by published package, every entry priced alone. Whole bundle: 665,308 kept → 372,660 emitted → 120,477 gz in 17 chunks.

Reconciliation with sheet 9. The two sheets do not meet at an identity, and the reason is a rule: on sheet 9 a chunk counts where it is first claimed, so ui-router-visualizer.esm sits inside app: vanilla rather than beside it. Straight from the two plates: sheet 9's vanilla district is 122,599 gz over 18 files; this bundle is 120,477 gz over 17 chunks; the residual is 2,122 gz over 1 file. That file is the one emitted asset in the app's output that is not a chunk — the api-viewer custom-elements manifest, JSON a module census structurally cannot see, since it walks bundle entries of type chunk. The app's stylesheet is not in the gap: sheet 9's pattern table files .css under site css before the app districts are reached. So 120,477 + 2,122 = 122,599, and the named residual is a manifest, not a rounding error.

The library is a skin over the machine. The biggest building in the bundle is not the router package — it is @uirouter/core at 26.3 KB gz, 22.3% of the wire, 64 modules. lit-ui-router itself is the small accent building: 4.6 KB, 3.9%, 11 modules. The two independent measurements reconcile: the codecov door prices the bare . entry at 5,609 gz with deps external, and this app's census pulls 4,691 of it — the 16% difference is what the app's own imports leave on the shelf.

The chrome outweighs the machine. marked, dompurify and @api-viewer total 26.7 KB gz — more than the routing machine they document — and the prebundled @uirouter/visualizer adds 24.1 KB on its own, opaque to tree-shaking because it arrives already bundled. None of it is on the eager path: the panel renders behind a feature flag and rides a lazy api-docs chunk. This census counts who occupies the bundle, not when they arrive; sheet 9 draws the critical path. One lit major serves all of it — 8.8 KB gz across 19 modules, no second copy riding in with the docs-viewer stack, because a scoped pnpm override (^3.3.3, a floor, not a pin) holds @api-viewer/* and lit-dialog to it.

The app's own district is the small one. lodash-es is 7.5 KB gz from 135 modules and 65.0 KB of kept source — isEqual's _base* family, the largest module count in the bundle and its own chunk, which is what four imports truly cost once tree-shaking has done its work. Beside it, the app's own source is 2.3 KB and sample-app-routes — the route table three apps import — is 292 bytes kept, 59 on the wire, one module: the smallest building on the map.

The runtime tax is near-zero. All bundler machinery — oxc decorator helpers, vite's preload helper and polyfill, a stray tslib — totals 4.6 KB kept, 1.2 KB gz, 0.7% of the kept source, in 4 modules. No duplicated-helper problem.

ALTITUDE 2⅞ — the same wire, cut by published package · every exported entry priced alone · 16 doors in 5 package quarters, footprint from minified bytes and height from gzipped, dependencies external — counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11)

GENERAL NOTES

Method: the same probe as sheet 10's doors strip, run to completion: every exported entry of the 5 publishable packages bundled alone with rolldown — minified, declared dependencies and peers external — which is the price a consumer's bundler pays at that door, and byte-for-byte the <pkg>-<label>-esm series CI uploads to codecov. Footprint is minified bytes, height gzipped. Every number is read at build time from the checked-in plate www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-doors.json — counted at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11), probed as git archive origin/main @ 65e2843 + corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile + tools/bundle-probe (rolldown, minify, declared deps+peers external, annotations off) — and a door the plate carries that the drawing does not place is a build error, not a stale constant. Sheet 10 is the unified view — one real app's bundle with all of these mixed by the bundler; this sheet cuts the same machinery by published package and entry point. The quarters don't sum and shouldn't: doors overlap (./pure is . minus registration), which is exactly what the split view exists to show.

The twin towers are one building with two doors. . and ./pure differ by 89 gzipped bytes — the whole cost of custom-element registration. The register economics run the other way: the two one-element doors sum to 3,553 gz while the umbrella ./register is 2,491, because each element door carries the shared element core with it. Take the umbrella or one element door; taking two per-element doors ships the core twice.

The server is a storefront, not a tower. Eight doors: an index at 4,965 gz, 644 under the client flagship; redirect and matcher wings at 3,597 and 2,838; and four framework adapters — hono, fetch, vite, connect — packed within 72 bytes of one another, which is what thin skins over one core look like priced. ./simulate, the test double, is 283 bytes, the cheapest door on the sheet.

Plugins price like footnotes. The entire mobx reactivity layer enters at 906 gz and the navigation-location plugin at 670 — each cheaper than the gap between ./register and its two element doors. The expensive thing in this family is never the adapter; it is the state machine they all defer to, and that machine (sheet 10's @uirouter/core) is external here by design.

The sixteenth door is not a door a browser opens. eslint-plugin-lit-ui-router (#676) is the family's fifth published package and the first non-runtime one, so its quarter is drawn but its number means something different: 9,703 minified, 3,510 gz is what a lint host loads, once, at author time. It is priced here because the probe prices every published entry without exception — the honest thing for a ledger — and it is worth knowing that the plugin costs 63% of the flagship to a tool that already has Node's whole module graph resident. Nothing in it ever reaches a bundle: it peers ESLint alone — oxlint loads it as a JS plugin, unpeered — never @uirouter/core (sheet 2 leaves it off the plate for the same reason).

Why both views exist. The split view is the seller's ledger — what each door costs at the threshold. The unified view is the buyer's receipt — what one app's bundler actually made of them (it paid 4,691 of the flagship's 5,609). Codecov tracks the ledger per commit; sheet 10 audits the receipt.

the REGISTER PLATE

ALTITUDE 3¼ — the monorepo as its CI reads it · every task node punched · surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) · turbo 2.10.12

GENERAL NOTES

Method. turbo run ci --dry=json and turbo run ci:main --dry=json against a materialized, installed archive of the ref — surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (2026-09-11) · turbo 2.10.12 — and the same for build, lint and pack:all in the schedule. Every number on the plate is read from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-plate.json, the checked-in snapshot census-plate.mjs writes; this sheet holds placement and prose only. A node is one (package, task) pair turbo placed in the graph. A node is command-bearing when its resolved command is not the literal <NONEXISTENT> — turbo's marker for a task it had to invent because something depends on it in that package. An edge is real only when both of its ends are. No duration is drawn anywhere: wall-clock comparisons here are confounded by cache state and by the task counts themselves, so this plate measures shape and nothing else.

Why an inventory and not a city. Sheet 3 argues that a task manager is not a place; drawing this graph in isometric would smuggle back the geography that sheet's note denies. What a CI graph actually is, is a register: a fixed set of names crossed against a fixed set of packages, with most of the intersections empty. The honest form is the plate that shape already implies — a punchcard, read by column.

The finding. 660 nodes; 195 run a command. 1,544 dependency edges; 73 join two real tasks. Of the 19 fanned names, 5 carry a ^self chain — build, build:types, test, test:coverage, transit — and a self-chain is what mints placeholders: turbo needs a node in every package to hang the chain on, whether or not that package has such a script. 3 names are 100% placeholder in all 35 packages: transit (which has no implementation anywhere in the repo — it exists purely as an edge), and the two roll-ups ci:pull_request and ci. The plate's rightmost columns and its leftmost are, in the strictest sense, empty.

Depth is mostly scaffolding too. The deepest chain is 13 nodes and 4 of them run anything. The longest chain of consecutive real nodes is 6 — and it is 6 test tasks in a row, serialized by ^test and nothing else: no task in that chain consumes an artifact from the one above it. That is the price of a self-chain used for ordering rather than for data flow, and it is what a plate makes visible that a node-and-arrow render never does.

What the plate is not evidence for. Placeholders are cheap — turbo schedules and skips them, and the phantom share is not a runtime cost. The argument is about legibility: 70% of what a maintainer sees in --graph output is scaffolding, and the two ratios worth watching are the real-node share per column and the real-edge count. Note also the one tier that never appears here at all: the repo's 13 cache:false definitions — four writers, six persistent servers, two live-network readers and one host-bound measurement (docs#check:embeds, #703) — are all outside every ci:* graph by design. A cache hit on any of them would be wrong, and the gate depends on their read-only twins instead (format:check for format).

The overlay. ci:main is not a different pipeline; it swallows ci:pull_request whole and adds 37 nodes across 4 names — ci:main, test:engines, test:matrix, check:pack — of which 5 are command-bearing. The main-branch graph is 6% larger and buys three engine tests, one d.ts back-test and one pack check.

Where the real edges are, and are not. The docs:api column is punched in every package it stands in: docs#build names its four producers directly rather than walking ^docs:api through devDependencies it never imports (#693). That is this plate's thesis arriving from the other side — scaffolding leaves the graph and the real work stays. It is also why real→real edges are a small fraction of 1,544: most edges land on a node that runs nothing.

the WEATHERING MAP

ALTITUDE t — the same city as sheet 7, surveyed in time · 347 files dated from the whole history · three construction seasons, 10 silent months · counted at origin/main @ 65e2843

GENERAL NOTES

Method — one pass, renames followed. Every date on this sheet is read at build time from the checked-in plate www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-weather.json, counted at origin/main @ 65e2843. Each file in the shared city universe was dated from a single git log --name-status -M pass over the history behind that ref, walked newest to oldest with rename chains followed backwards — equivalent to per-file --follow (spot-verified against it, including tools/shared/workspace.ts, which the plain path log mis-dates by a week) but one process instead of 347. Per file: first-commit date, last-touch date, touch count. Merge commits list no files under the default log, so a touch is a non-merge commit — the standard convention. TODAY is not a wall-clock date: it is the measured ref's own commit date, 2026-09-11, so every age and idle figure below is reproducible from the sha rather than from the day the sheet was drawn. Footprints come from sheet 7's plate, www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-city.json, reused as pure geometry so the two sheets reconcile by eye — and by count: 347 dated files here against the same 347 there.

The bands are campaigns, not round numbers. The age histogram is not a slope, it is three spikes: files born around day 418 (July 2025), around day 244 (January 2026), and within the last 70 days — with nothing between them, because the repo has source births or touches in only 5 of its 15 calendar months. So the map bins by season, where the distribution actually cuts: SEASON I, the port — 26 files that arrived 2025-07-21 with the upstream sample-app lineage; SEASON II, the winter works — 18 files including the typedoc plugin and the examples; SEASON III, the summer — 303 files, 87% of the city, none older than 2026-07-04. Churn tiers come from the per-block distribution the same way: touches-per-file has a clean gap between 4.65 and 6.0, so HOT is ≥6; the per-file median is 2, so the COLD tier sits below it. SEALED is idle >180 days — the idle histogram is empty from 70 to 236, and 6 files sit beyond the gap.

The verdict: age and churn run opposite ways. Mean touches per file falls monotonically with youth — ×10.5 for the port cohort, ×5.9 for winter, ×2.7 for summer — and 108 of 347 files (31%) have been touched exactly once, ever. The port's masonry is not museum stone: ui-sref.ts is at ×18 with the last chisel-mark dated 2026-09-02, and the two most-weathered walls in the city are the port-era www/lit-ui-router.dev/.vitepress pair — config.ts at ×29 and vite.config.ts at ×25. What survives from the first day is precisely what keeps being worked.

What each district's weather says. The instrument yard — 7,657 sloc, the city's largest district by mass — logged zero touches before 2026 and is almost entirely summer stone: infrastructure arrived late, fast, and mostly settled on the first cut. Its one winter building is also the map's sealed wing: the typedoc plugin's symbols/ trio, untouched 246 days. The shopfront splits in two: docs runs the hottest multi-file block-average in the city (×9.4/f src) while examples holds the oldest untouched stone — two vite configs idle 254 days. And the smallest building on the map has the sharpest weather: navigation-location-plugin's single January wall has been chiselled 10 times, the highest per-file churn anywhere — matching its history as the extracted plugin that every routing change touches.

See also — appendix A1, THE SPRITE STUDY. This map draws age and churn flat, as fills and edges, so the dating stays readable at city scale. The sprited reading of the same two measurements — wreck & ruin ↔ shine & splendor on the building itself — is the research filed as appendix A1, and its recommendation is what sheet 7B draws.

Approximations, so the numbers stay honest. Dates are author dates (%as); on this repo's squash-merge convention they equal the merge day of the PR that landed the change. Rename detection is git's -M heuristic: a file moved and rewritten in one commit can read as a fresh birth — the July 2026 scripts/ → tools/ graduations are dated to that graduation where git saw no rename, which the yard's notes above already state as its story. Generated and vendored trees were never in the universe (the shared city rules); nothing else was excluded.

KEY

the ALTITUDE ATLAS — DRAWING SETSHEET 14 / 14

the SURVEY OFFICE

ALTITUDE 3½ — the atlas measuring itself · 17 probes, 17 plates, 20 drawings · every station, plate and edge on this sheet introspected from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/generator/ at build time · all plates pinned to origin/main @ 65e2843 · commit 2026-09-11

GENERAL NOTES

Method — the sheet surveys its own drawer. Every station, drawer, tab and edge on this plate is introspected at build time by www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/generator/census-atlas.mjs: a probe is any census-*.mjs that writes a plate; a shared instrument is one the probes import (there are two — basis.mjs and census-query.mjs); a tier is decided by which basis primitive the source actually calls — materialize alone is T1, historyLog is T2, installDeps is T3; and a reader is any generator file that constructs the plate's URL. The introspection throws rather than draws if a plate has anything but exactly one writer, if a probe names a plate that is not filed, if a drawing reads a plate nothing writes, or — the claim this sheet makes loudest — if the 17 filed plates disagree about the ref they were measured at. They do not: all 17 are pinned to origin/main @ 65e2843 · commit 2026-09-11. What is editorial here is what is editorial on every sheet: placement, the short basis labels, and this prose.

The hero is the fan-out. One scc --by-file pass over the archive produces census-files.json, 657 rows of per-file measurement, and thirteen things read it: twelve stations that are group-by queries over the same rows — census-bricks.mjs, census-city.mjs, census-couplings.mjs, census-doors.mjs, census-handoff.mjs, census-loop.mjs, census-npm.mjs, census-shadow.mjs, census-steam.mjs, census-weather.mjs, census-yard.mjs, census-overview.mjs — plus the gallery cover. That is the architecture's whole argument in one edge bundle: the city census, the yard census, the brick census, the weather map and the steam channel cannot disagree about how many files there are, because there is only one count. Cross-sheet totals reconcile by construction, not by discipline.

Three tiers, and what each one costs. eight stations are T1 — the archive measured once, or a query over that measurement. two are T2: one git log over the same ref, with the window and «today» derived from the ref's own commit date. seven are T3, and they are the expensive half of the office: the archive is not just extracted but installed — corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, then the tree's own node_modules/.bin/turbo invoked directly — so that turbo dry-runs, node_modules closures, vite and rolldown builds all measure the ref rather than a checkout. The harness bar above the T3 band is the only sub-instrument drawn, because it is the only one that changes what a measurement means.

Five guarantees the office is built to hold. The basis is one git archive per ref — the tracked set exactly as git defines it, so no probe keeps a skip list. Members are discovered from the archive's own workspace file, so a package that graduated after a sheet was drawn is still counted rather than silently zero. Numbers travel as filed plates read by lookups that throw on a missing row, never by clipboard. Every date is derived from the measured commit, so a rebuild ages nothing against the day it runs. And every input is scripted: seven execution probes and a registry probe, nothing out of band. One relic sits in the drawer drawn struck through — census.mjs, a working-tree walker imported by nothing and writing no plate.

What the drawing does not show, and the schedule does. With 17 drawers and 19 reading sheets, a complete edge render would be unreadable, so the drawing keeps the shape — one horizontal writes edge per station, a bundled accent bus for the master plate, thin curves for the rest — and the plate schedule carries the facts: writer, tier, basis and every reader, for all 17 plates. Two counts are worth reading off it. Zero plates are unread: every filed measurement is on a drawing somewhere. And four of the atlas's 23 sheets have no plate behind them — sheet 5, sheet 6, sheet 14, sheet A1 — because they draw arguments, mechanisms and metering that no census produces. This sheet is honestly among them: it has no plate of its own; it reads the generator.

Why a flow graph and not a city. Sheet 3 refuses to draw a task manager as a place, and the same refusal applies here. A pipeline's truth is dataflow — ref to archive to measurement to plate to drawing — and the lego/containment vocabulary the atlas uses elsewhere would encode a claim about what contains what, which is exactly the wrong claim about a pipeline. The vocabulary that fits is the one the atlas already owns: probes as survey instruments, snapshots as filed plates, sheets as finished drawings. Tier is station type; the cabinet is a cabinet; the rack is a rack. The node and edge arrays behind this drawing (69 nodes over four kinds, 95 edges over writes, reads and imports) are also the data model the interactive lane mounts — the picture is a query, not a hand-drawing.

ALTITUDE 3¼ — sheet 12's plate, live under the pointer · the whole ci graph carried node by node · 660 NODES · 195 RUN A COMMAND · 1,544 EDGES · 73 JOIN TWO REAL TASKS · surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (commit 2026-09-11) · turbo 2.10.12

BASIS — turbo run ci --dry=json against a materialized, installed archive of origin/main @ 65e2843 (commit 2026-09-11) · turbo 2.10.12 · all 660 nodes and 1,544 edges read verbatim from www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-plate.json's graphNodes / graphEdges and embedded here unaggregated; columns ranked from those edges at build time and drawn with cytoscape preset — no physics, so the picture is the same on every load.

GENERAL NOTES

Method — what is drawn, and from where. Everything on this page comes out of www/atlas.lit-ui-router.dev/data/census-plate.json, the checked-in plate generator/census-plate.mjs writes from turbo run ci --dry=json against a materialized, installed archive of the ref — surveyed at origin/main @ 65e2843 (commit 2026-09-11) · turbo 2.10.12. Sheet 12 reads that plate's cell codes and tallies; this sheet reads the plate's two full-graph fields, graphNodes and graphEdges: one (package, task) pair per line, sorted by task id, and one [dependency, dependent] index pair per line into that array. The whole graph is carried — all 660 nodes and all 1,544 edges, unaggregated — and it is embedded in this page verbatim, so what the pointer walks is the measurement itself and not a summary of it. The lane cross-checks the two readings at build time and throws rather than drawing if the node list and the tally disagree about how many nodes, real nodes, edges or real edges there are.

The shroud, defined. A node is real — command-bearing — when turbo resolved it to an actual command. A phantom is a node whose command is the literal <NONEXISTENT>: a placeholder turbo mints so that a ^task chain has something in that package to hang an edge on. The default view here is the real subgraph alone — 195 nodes and the 73 edges that join two of them. PHANTOM SHROUD floods in the other 465 nodes and 1,471 edges, faint, and that flood is the 70.5% figure sheet 12 prints: the share of this graph a maintainer reads in --graph output that runs nothing at all. Untick it and the real subgraph comes back unchanged — the shroud is a visibility swap over one fixed layout, never a re-layout.

Layout — ranked from the edges, computed at build time. Rows are the 36 packages in sheet 12's own block order (publishable, apps, docs and examples, tools, root), so the two plates read the same way down the page. Columns are the 51 task names, and their order is not editorial: each column is ranked by the longest dependency depth any of its nodes reaches, which sorts the graph into its real stages — gather, emit, check, prove, roll-up — out of the edge list rather than out of a hand-written list. Positions are computed here and drawn with cytoscape preset: no physics, so the picture is identical on every load and a node is always in the same place when you come back to it. Four column heads are drawn in red because not one node in them runs anything at all: lint:workflows, transit, ci:pull_request, ci — and in the default view those columns are not drawn, because there is nothing real in them to draw.

Sprites. Two skins, authored to the house recipe — the girding frame drawn first and a semi-opaque wall washed over it, so the frame reads through and the themed node body tints the building. A real task is a works shed with a lit door. A phantom is the plot without the building: a dashed frame, no wall, no roof — it cannot be mistaken for work at any zoom. Both palettes are baked at build time and swapped with the page's theme, the survey office's pattern exactly.

What this shows that the plate cannot. Sheet 12 proves the phantom share as a ratio; here it is a shape. With the shroud off, the 195 real tasks fall into a handful of dense columns and the 73 real edges are sparse enough to trace one by one — the deepest all-real run is 6 test tasks, serialized by ^test and consuming nothing from each other. With the shroud on, the same picture disappears into 660 nodes and 1,544 edges of scaffolding. Hover any building for its package, its task, whether it runs, whether a cache hit would be wrong (0 nodes in this graph are cache:false — the repo's uncacheable tier is outside every ci:* graph by design, which is sheet 12's finding, here as an empty field), its in and out degree in both readings, and the full list of what it waits on.

What is editorial. The row blocks and their order; the pitch, the sprite drawing and the colours; this prose. The nodes, the edges, the column ranking, every count and every name are the plate's.
